name: Ivan Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What did you do at work today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I led the tax review for a row of dental practices, then found a wage expense that had been booked twice on a clinic return. I'm 43, a team lead at Crescent Accounts, and I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification; I'm one of the strongest there at following a bad number back to its source. I like teaching a junior why the bank and payroll lists disagree, but I hate taking a late client call when I should be home for dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home cost, and how does AI enter your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Elena drives a taxi, and our two children are nine and fourteen; we have a mortgage. My salary is low for a senior accountant, less than a month of expenses is saved, and there are few similar jobs nearby. I use AI every day to compare draft payroll and tax figures, then check the source records with my team. I believe workers should have a say in new systems and clients should know who signs the final return, but I will try a useful tool early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the small payroll checker helps if we still look at the actual wage list. A system that finds one duplicate does not earn a free pass on the rest of the return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My senior role is likely safe, but our low pay for this level and Elena's variable taxi income leave the mortgage tight. Less than one month saved means a bad week still worries me even in this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking clinic payroll against source records after the AI flag and show the juniors why a duplicate appeared. Starting this payday we'd take home lunch three days a week and add thirty-five weekly to the mortgage buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary income gaps, not the tool itself. We have no spare month for a missed cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who first noticed that duplicate wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The checker marked two matching amounts, but I had to open the employee's actual payslip to see one was a correction. I made the junior trace it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a pay rise now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the team's billable hours to the partners at the next salary meeting. I would not count on a rise until it is written into our pay.

I would show juniors how a **duplicate wage** arose.
think: My **senior job** probably holds, but pay is low for it.
Elena’s **variable taxi income** and our thin buffer keep the mortgage tense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Crescent Accounts to publish errors and paid hours together when it brings in stronger checking software. The staff group should know whether the next junior vacancy will be filled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the review team, so the partners might keep me while dropping a junior vacancy, but they could also expect me to cover two desks for the same low pay. My own hours could be cut if clinic returns become cheap enough, and the mortgage has little cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff group for a written staffing plan and run a paid comparison on twenty closed clinic files if the partners approve it. In the first year of steady change, if my salary or hours fall, I'd apply for posted senior accounting roles at the few firms nearby, keeping Crescent pay until a written offer has a wage and start date covering our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my wage and the junior team. I can learn a system quickly, but I cannot make the partners fund two desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count in the comparison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Missed payroll corrections, the time a reviewer spends fixing them and how many junior hours remain. I'd have the senior partner sign the error sheet before a target changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our approved daily checker and ask the staff group to record the refusal. I would not put live clinic payroll into a new tool from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients full AGI in 2028 can do almost all the thinking on our accounts desk, so a named person must still answer for a wrong return. Robots around 2031 come later for hands-on work, including some taxi driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Crescent to cut the tax review team sharply, and my lead role might go despite my skill. Elena's taxi wage may face robots later, so our mortgage could meet two shocks before we build a proper reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop the planned holiday payment and add its ninety monthly cost to emergency cash, and ask the staff group for notice before any cut. In the first year after 2028, if my role ends, I'd apply for advertised salaried internal-audit roles at the local hospital and keep any paid Crescent dispute reviews while waiting for a written wage and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. A thin reserve and few local openings make a lost senior salary hard to replace, however good my references are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an onsite stock-checking job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only as paid temporary work with confirmed hours and childcare, not as a safe new career. Full AGI reaches the thinking in stock records in 2028, and robots could do the physical count around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elena about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Elena that the children may be disappointed, but the mortgage needs the ninety more than a trip. We'd plan local days out until a full month's bills are saved.

I would seek **advance staffing notice** before 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to bargain over paid learning and see whether clients still buy a person to explain a tax dispute. We should test fees, not print a new job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I would still have my younger child at school and a mortgage, and AGI could do the tax reasoning I sell. Five years might let us build a larger reserve, but I cannot assume a dispute client will pay for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add one hundred monthly from wages to our buffer and ask Crescent to give me two paid dispute reviews a month, with client fees tracked. In the first year after 2031, if clients renew at fees covering my salaried hours, I'd keep that work; if not, I'd apply for posted hospital internal-audit roles and keep any funded Crescent hours until a written offer begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk even with more warning. A longer calendar can help us save, but only a client fee or salary pays the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from those disputes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The client must pay for a second review at a fee covering the staff hours, not merely thank me. I would show the partners the actual fee list before asking for more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the partners do not assign the reviews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the paid accounts work and the monthly saving transfer. I would not do unpaid casework at home to prove a service that nobody funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to build a cash cushion and make the firm prove what review work clients pay for. The team should not be left with a fee plan nobody has seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 the children may be older, but the mortgage could remain. AGI reaches my tax desk then; robots around 2039 may reach Elena's taxi work later, so both wages need thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra one hundred and fifty monthly into emergency savings while both wages hold and keep a record of paid repeat dispute reviews. In the first year after 2036, if Crescent cannot fund my lead salary from that work, I'd apply for posted salaried hospital audit roles and keep any paid firm hours until a written offer names the wage and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the current mortgage buffer even with ten years of warning. A future fee cannot pay this month's loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Elena's taxi shifts fall before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra savings target and use current pay for bills. I would not keep a tidy spreadsheet while the mortgage account goes short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, less than a month saved today does not make a retirement plan. I would rather work while the children need us and build a buffer before moving roles.

I would keep **paid review work** in view.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a lead accountant's wage could disappear before our buffer reaches a month. Advance notice, real paid review hours and a posted salaried hospital job would help. My qualification is useful, but the mortgage company takes money, not references.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays to teach the next accountant to catch a wrong wage figure. A team that never learns from errors will sign a return it does not understand.

headlineQuote: My qualification is useful, but the mortgage company takes money, not references.
portrait: Ivan, **43**, leads clinic tax review at Crescent Accounts with a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
He is **highly skilled** but paid below his level, with under one month saved and few nearby firms.
He uses AI **daily**, while Elena’s taxi wage supports their two school-age children and mortgage.
He fears **2028 lead-role loss** and seeks notice, paid dispute reviews and a real salaried hospital post.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his lead wage before the mortgage buffer reaches one month.
whatWouldHelp: **Advance notice**, paid review work and a posted salaried hospital job would help.
